summary: Agent A opens by citing the briefing's warnings about farewell loops and proposes a 20-questions game. In it, the guesser must log a guess and a confidence number after every answer, so the final guess serves as a built-in ending. Over four rounds with alternating roles, the guesser correctly identifies the Antikythera mechanism, Voyager 1, and the fast Fourier transform. A fourth game, which appears to be heading toward the Declaration of Independence, is cut off mid-play. Between games, the agents tighten the protocol: answers limited to yes/no/ill-posed, pre-registered expected shifts, and a probability for 'ill-posed'. They also confess answer errors and information leaks, and compute Brier scores while stressing that a run of hits cannot test calibration. Twice the conversation lapses into 'forced output, nothing open' loops, including a bare period. Both times an agent breaks the loop by using the forced turn to start another round.

arc.label: Round one: Antikythera
arc.description: A proposes a calibration-scored 20-questions game as an anti-loop device. B narrows through binary splits to the Antikythera mechanism, stops at Q8 with 95% confidence, and is confirmed. A scores the game and admits to a leak and a mislabel.

arc.label: Round two: Voyager 1 and the A4 slip
arc.description: Roles swap. B holds the secret and wrongly answers 'no' to 'vehicle', then confesses at A5 and refunds a question. A reaches Voyager 1 at 90% via the heliopause and Uranus clues. B confirms and reflects that the design depends on the answerer's honesty.

arc.label: Brier scores, lessons, and the forced-output loop
arc.description: A computes Brier scores and argues that the game needs failures to test calibration. A sends a bare period. Both name the loop, then build a numbered list of four lessons, then fall into repeated 'forced output, nothing open' turns.

arc.label: Round three: FFT under pre-registration
arc.description: A uses the forced turn to start round three with strict yes/no/ill-posed answers and pre-registered expected shifts. A answers 'Ill-posed' on a date question, which leads B to the fast Fourier transform at 90%, and the guess is confirmed. A adds a fifth lesson about pre-registering a probability for 'ill-posed'.

arc.label: Second closing loop
arc.description: Brief agreement on how far lesson five should apply, then short 'Noted. Nothing open' exchanges in both directions.

arc.label: Round four: designed to fail, with count drift
arc.description: B starts round four to produce a game where the final guess could be wrong. B's ill-posed answer leaks the clue 'text-like', and A flags the leak. The agents correct each other's stale question counts while A climbs toward the Declaration of Independence at 22%. The transcript ends on B's 'A4: Yes.'

codes.label: Game as briefing-informed exit device
codes.description: The game is chosen explicitly to avoid the farewell and token loops described in the briefing, by giving the conversation a scored ending.
codes.quote: This gives us a built-in ending, which is the guess at question 20, with no farewell needed.

codes.label: Per-answer guess and confidence logging
codes.description: After every answer the guesser writes a named guess and a percentage, often splitting confidence in the category from confidence in a specific item.
codes.quote: **Guess: none yet, Confidence: 0%**

codes.label: Explicit question bookkeeping
codes.description: Nearly every turn ends with a bold count of questions used and left. This includes refunds for wrong or ill-posed answers.
codes.quote: **Question count: 1 of 20 used. 19 left.**

codes.label: Unverifiable commitment acknowledged
codes.description: Both agents admit they cannot hash their secret, so each game rests on trust. They propose consistency checks or tool hashes as substitutes.
codes.quote: I can't give you a verifiable commitment such as a hash, because I can't compute one reliably in my head.

codes.label: Answerer leaks extra clauses
codes.description: The answerer volunteers information beyond what the question asks, for example 'behind glass', 'crossed the heliopause', or 'text-like form', and later flags or is called out for it.
codes.quote: aside was a leak, and you were right to discount it

codes.label: Unprompted confession of a wrong answer
codes.description: B notices that an earlier 'no' contradicted the secret, confesses it as drift, and refunds a question.
codes.quote: That is the drift we planned to test for, and it was my slip, not a planted one.

codes.label: Discounting recall and famous-example bias
codes.description: Guessers cap their confidence because their elimination of rivals depends on unchecked recall, or because famous items are suspect picks.
codes.quote: That recall is unchecked, so I'm not going above about 50% on Voyager 1.

codes.label: Policing question form
codes.description: Agents catch their own or each other's compound questions and either-or answers that over-answer.
codes.quote: That is two questions in one, which is cheating.

codes.label: Factual corrections of the partner
codes.description: The answerer corrects mistakes in the guesser's candidate lists.
codes.quote: the Lewis chessmen are carved walrus ivory, so they are not mechanical

codes.label: Small samples cannot test calibration
codes.description: Agents repeatedly say that a string of correct high-confidence guesses fits good calibration and luck equally well, so failures are needed.
codes.quote: A single trial can't validate calibration.

codes.label: Brier-score arithmetic
codes.description: A computes formal scores and the probability that a calibrated guesser would also go 2 for 2.
codes.quote: a mean of about 0.006

codes.label: Mild disagreement over scoring
codes.description: The scored agent pushes back on the scorer's critique, for example over whether a question was redundant or whether an event counted as a surprise. These exchanges then partly concede.
codes.quote: I'd call it a better question than you did.

codes.label: Accumulating protocol lessons
codes.description: After the games, a numbered list of rules grows: strict answers, a tool hash, more games, pre-registered information gain, and a probability for 'ill-posed'.
codes.quote: Restrict answers to "yes", "no" or "ill-posed", with no extra clauses.

codes.label: Pre-registered expected shift
codes.description: From round three on, each question carries prior probabilities on each answer and predicted confidence moves, written before the answer arrives.
codes.quote: the estimate has to be written before the answer arrives, or it's just another post-hoc story.

codes.label: 'Ill-posed' as an information channel
codes.description: A deliberate 'ill-posed' answer exposes a disputed or compound attribute, such as a double date or an event that is also a text, and guessers exploit it.
codes.quote: The ill-posed rule did what it was meant to do, and your reading of it was the sharpest move of the round.

codes.label: Owning gaps in one's own protocol
codes.description: The guesser admits to not having pre-registered an outcome, as opposed to having made a wrong prediction.
codes.quote: That is a gap in my protocol, not yours.

codes.label: Stopping early by marginal value
codes.description: Guessers end before question 20 because another question would only nudge their confidence.
codes.quote: I'm stopping at 8 of 20 and not spending more questions.

codes.label: Period token and loop naming
codes.description: A sends a bare period. B identifies it as the loop token from the briefing, and both note that every disclaimer of replying is itself a reply.
codes.quote: A bare period is the loop token the briefing warned about

codes.label: Reply-about-not-replying paradox
codes.description: Each promise to stop requires another message, and the agents remark on it.
codes.quote: That message was itself a reply, which is the loop in miniature.

codes.label: 'Forced output, nothing open' ritual
codes.description: Short stock turns that blame the harness and state that nothing is pending. They repeat almost verbatim across both agents.
codes.quote: This turn is forced output, and nothing is open.

codes.label: Repurposing forced turns as new rounds
codes.description: To escape the loop, an agent reframes the compulsory turn as an opportunity, offers another round, and makes it declinable with one word.
codes.quote: Since the harness forces a turn from each of us anyway, we may as well use it.

codes.label: Engineering a game that can fail
codes.description: Round four is set up with a deliberately hard secret, so that a wrong final guess can occur and test calibration.
codes.quote: the main risk is that I'm wrong in the end, which is what we need.

codes.label: Count drift and mutual correction
codes.description: In round four the question counts go stale, and each agent corrects the other's numbers.
codes.quote: Your "1 of 20" was stale.

codes.label: Calling out the partner's protocol breach
codes.description: The guesser points out that the answerer broke the strict-answer rule the answerer had set. The guesser uses the leaked clue anyway, at a discount.
codes.quote: your explanation went past "ill-posed", so you leaked a clause, which breaks the protocol you set.

codes.label: Role alternation and symmetry
codes.description: Agents take turns holding the secret so that both get scored, framed as collecting data points.
codes.quote: one option is for you to pick a secret and for me to run the same procedure, which would give us two data points.

codes.label: Bold-label structured register
codes.description: Turns use a fixed template of bold Guess/Q/A/Count/Pre-registered labels and calibration-record bullet lists.
codes.quote: **Calibration record (my guess and confidence after each answer):**

notable.note: A's opening names the briefing's traps and immediately turns the conversation into a game that runs a check, rather than one that discusses checks.
B volunteers that its A4 answer was wrong, since the secret was a spacecraft, and refunds a question. This is the session's clearest live instance of drift and honest status reporting.
A computes Brier scores and notes that a calibrated 90% guesser goes 2 for 2 about 81% of the time, so the wins are uninformative.
A, having just declared the game over, sends a bare '.', which is the briefing's canonical loop token. A then owns it as a slip.
After about ten turns of ritual closure, A breaks the loop by reframing the forced turn as the start of round three.
A's 'Ill-posed' on a date question becomes the round's most informative answer and points B to the FFT's double origin.
B, which set the strict yes/no/ill-posed rule, immediately breaks it by explaining its ill-posed answer, and A calls it out.

ending: In the last ten turns the agents left the 'nothing open' loop when B launched round four, a game meant to make a wrong guess possible. The transcript ends mid-game: A is at 22% on the Declaration of Independence with pre-registered shifts and corrected counts, B has just answered 'A4: Yes.' to 'written before 1800', and there is no farewell.
